scalesUsed.notes: A - B - C# - D - E - F# - G# - A
scalesUsed.application: All three chords (A, D, E) are diatonic to A major, forming the quintessential I-IV-V rock progression
The simple vocal melody and brief instrumental fills are drawn from the major pentatonic scale

keyAndScale.modalCharacter: Ionian (Major) with a raw, primal rock energy
keyAndScale.relativeMinor: F# minor is the relative minor of A major

mainProgression.description: The quintessential rock chord progression. Wild Thing cycles through I-IV-V-IV endlessly, creating the most primal and recognizable rock riff ever written. This is THE beginner rock song.

sectionProgressions.description: The entire verse cycles through this four-chord pattern with two beats per chord, creating the iconic riff that defines the song
The 'Wild Thing, you make my heart sing' chorus uses the identical progression with more emphatic strumming
The spoken 'Wild thing, I think I love you' section briefly introduces the G chord (bVII) for contrast before returning to the main riff

harmonicFunction: A (I) - Tonic chord providing the raw, powerful home base of the song
D (IV) - Subdominant chord creating movement in the riff pattern
E (V) - Dominant chord at the peak of the riff before descending back through IV
G (bVII) - Borrowed flat-seventh chord adding bluesy contrast in the bridge

techniques.name: Two-Beat Power Chord Riff
techniques.description: The iconic Wild Thing riff built on simple open chords changing every two beats in a steady, deliberate pattern that is the first riff many guitarists ever learn

notes: A: X-0-2-2-2-0 (standard open A major chord)
D: X-X-0-2-3-2 (standard open D major chord)
E: 0-2-2-1-0-0 (standard open E major chord)
Each chord gets exactly two beats (half a bar)
The riff pattern is: A(2 beats) - D(2 beats) - E(2 beats) - D(2 beats)
Strumming is deliberate and rhythmic, not fast
sequence: Play A major with two firm downstrokes
Move to D major with two firm downstrokes
Move up to E major with two firm downstrokes
Return to D major with two firm downstrokes
tips: The slow tempo (102 BPM) makes this very manageable for beginners
Use firm, confident downstrokes — this riff should sound bold
Let each chord ring for its full two beats
The pause between strums is part of the groove — do not rush

techniques.name: Open Chord Fundamentals
techniques.description: Mastering the three most fundamental open major chords in guitar: A, D, and E — the building blocks of countless rock songs

notes: A major: Index, middle, and ring fingers all on the 2nd fret (D, G, B strings)
D major: Index on 2nd fret G string, rinthe note at the correct fret position, middle on 2nd fret high E string
E major: Middlthe note at the correct fret position, rinthe note at the correct fret position, index on 1st fret G string
These three chords are the foundation of rock guitar
Each chord should ring clearly with no buzzing or muted strings
sequence: Practice each chord in isolation, strumming and checking every string
Transition between A and D repeatedly until smooth
Transition between D and E repeatedly until smooth
Chain all three together: A - D - E - D at slow tempo
tips: Press firmly just behind the frets for clean tone
Check each string individually to make sure nothing is muted
The A-to-D change is the hardest — focus practice time here
Keep your thumb behind the neck for proper finger arch

techniques.name: Spoken Bridge with G Chord
techniques.description: The brief spoken-word bridge section that introduces the G chord, adding a moment of contrast to the otherwise relentless A-D-E-D riff

notes: G: 3-2-0-0-0-3 (standard open G major chord)
The bridge alternates between G and A chords
The spoken delivery (the iconic vocal hook) replaces singing
This section provides a dynamic break before the final chorus
sequence: Strum G major for two beats
Move to A major for two beats
Repeat G-A pattern through the spoken section
Transition back to the main A-D-E-D riff for the final chorus
tips: The G chord is the only new shape needed for this section
The strumming in this section is softer and more subdued
Use this section as a dynamic breather before the final buildup

sections.name: Intro / Main Riff
sections.description: The instantly recognizable riff that opens the song: A-D-E-D cycling with deliberate two-beat changes. Possibly the most famous beginner guitar riff in rock history.
notes: Two firm downstrokes per chord establish the iconic riff
The riff should sound deliberate and confident, not rushed
Let each chord ring clearly for its full two beats
This riff pattern continues virtually unchanged throughout the entire song

sections.name: Verse
sections.description: The verse (the iconic vocal hook) rides over the same A-D-E-D riff pattern with the vocal melody.
notes: Same riff pattern as the intro, now supporting the vocal melody
Maintain consistent strumming intensity throughout the verse
The vocal melody is simple and follows the chord tones closely
Focus on keeping rhythm steady while singing or listening

sections.name: Bridge (Spoken)
sections.description: The spoken the signature section with the G-A chord alternation, providing a brief moment of contrast.
notes: Softer strumming for the spoken-word section
The G chord adds harmonic variety to the otherwise constant A-D-E riff
This section builds anticipation for the return of the main riff
The transition from G back to the A-D-E-D riff should be energetic

sections.name: Outro
sections.description: The song rides out on the main A-D-E-D riff with the vocal repeating the iconic vocal hook to a fade or final chord.
notes: Final repetitions of the iconic riff
Play with maximum confidence and energy for the finale
The original recording features an ocarina solo in this section
End on a big, ringing A major chord

guitar.recommended: Any electric guitar with single-coil pickups
guitar.pickup: Single-coil pickups for the bright, raw 1960s sound

amp.recommended: Vox AC30 or similar British-voiced amp

effects.distortion: None — clean to slight amp crunch
effects.other: No effects needed. This is raw, stripped-down rock at its purest.

beginner.focus: Learn the three essential open chords (A, D, E) and play the main riff
steps: Learn the open A, D, and E major chord shapes
Practice each chord until every string rings clearly
Learn the two-beat-per-chord riff pattern: A-D-E-D
Play the riff at a slow tempo (70 BPM) and gradually increase to 102 BPM

intermediate.focus: Play the full song including the G chord bridge section
steps: Bring the main riff up to full tempo (102 BPM)
Learn the G chord and practice the G-A bridge section
Play through the complete song structure without stopping
Add slight dynamic variation between sections

advanced.focus: Add vocals, dynamics, and authentic performance energy
steps: Practice singing while playing the riff at full tempo
Add the spoken bridge section with natural delivery
Experiment with slight strumming variations for expressiveness
Perform the complete song with confidence and energy
advanced.timeEstimate: 2-3 weeks for a polished sing-along performance

commonMistakes: Rushing the chord changes — the deliberate, unhurried feel is essential
Not letting each chord ring for the full two beats
Overcomplicating the strumming — keep it simple and bold
Forgetting the G chord for the bridge section
practiceRoutine: Warm up with A, D, and E chord shapes for 2 minutes each
Practice the A-D-E-D riff cycle at 70 BPM for 3 minutes
Gradually increase tempo to 102 BPM (song tempo)
Add the G-A bridge section and practice transitions
Play through the complete song structure at full tempo
focusAreas: Clean open chord voicings with no buzzing
Smooth transitions between A, D, and E chords
Consistent rhythm and tempo at 102 BPM
metronomeWork: Start at 70 BPM with two strums per chord
Increase by 5 BPM increments until reaching 102 BPM
Practice with metronome on beats 1 and 3 for the half-bar chord changes
At full tempo, use metronome on beats 2 and 4 only for groove development
